subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: writing a short usage policy [Action]
passage: On Thursday afternoon in a co-working space in Nairobi, Omar opened a blank page titled 'How we use AI tools' and asked Jin to write it with him. First came the tools the company had licensed. Second, data: no customer records, no keys, no unreleased plans. Third was a rule they argued over for ten minutes and kept: a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code. They held it to one page and printed it, and Omar added a line asking people to say when AI had helped. On Monday, Jin slipped the page into the new-joiner pack. The next hire, a graduate called Wanjiru, read it over coffee and asked two questions that made them add a sentence.

qa.q: Which rule did Omar and Jin argue over for ten minutes and keep?
qa.a: They kept the rule that a person reads every AI-written change before it goes into the main code.

qa.q: What does Omar want from the extra line about saying when AI helped?
qa.a: Omar is cautious about AI-written changes and wants openness, so reviewers know which changes need a closer look.

qa.q: What could the team do to keep the policy alive?
qa.a: They could review the page every few months, since tools and habits change and a fixed page gets out of date.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru see the page in the first days?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably finds it helpful and short enough to read, since two questions led to one added sentence.

grounding: Shows a team writing a one-page guideline on approved tools, data handling and human review of AI-written changes, then sharing it with new joiners.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: writing a short usage policy [Action]
passage:
On her first day at the analytics firm, Mehak sat in the small training room with four other new joiners. After the laptop setup and the fire exits, Amandeep from the platform team handed out a single printed page titled 'How we use AI tools here'.
'It's one page on purpose,' Amandeep said. 'Three parts. Which tools are approved: only the two on this list, with company accounts. What data you may put in: public data and your own code, never client files or passwords. And the rule we don't bend: a person reads and approves every AI-assisted change before it's merged.'
Mehak raised her hand. 'What if I'm not sure about some data?'
'Then it's a no until you ask me. My name is at the bottom.'
She folded the page into her new notebook.

qa.a: Only the two on the list, with company accounts.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt receiving the page on her first day?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt relieved to have clear rules early, and confident enough to ask about grey areas.

qa.q: What else could the team do to keep the guideline useful?
qa.a: They could review it every few months as tools change and add common questions from new joiners.

qa.q: How might clients be affected by this guideline?
qa.a: Their files never go into AI tools and every change is reviewed, which protects their data and the quality of the work.

grounding: It shows a team sharing a one-page guideline on approved tools, data handling and human review of every AI-assisted change during onboarding.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: writing a short usage policy [Action]
passage:
Subject: Our AI usage page, please read before Monday

Hi Lalit,
Since you missed Thursday's meeting, here's what we agreed, in the same one-page form we'll give every new joiner.
1. Approved tools: the two licensed through the company. No personal accounts for work.
2. Data: never paste client documents, personal data or credentials into any tool. Public information and our own non-secret code are fine.
3. Review: every change an AI tool helped write is read and approved by a person before it goes live. 'The tool wrote it' is not a reason to skip review.
4. When unsure, ask me first.
I know you've been using a free tool at home for scripts. That's your call at home, but at work, please switch to the approved one from Monday.
Thanks,
Disha

qa.q: What should Lalit switch to from Monday?
qa.a: The approved tool, instead of the free one.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel reading the line about the free tool?
qa.a: Lalit might feel a bit awkward or defensive at first, but also clear about what's expected.

qa.q: What else could Disha do to help Lalit switch smoothly?
qa.a: Disha could offer a short session on the approved tool, so switching doesn't slow Lalit's work.

qa.q: How might new joiners benefit from this page?
qa.a: They get the same clear rules from day one, so they don't have to guess about data or review.

grounding: It shows a team writing a one-page guideline on approved tools, data handling and human review of every AI-assisted change, shared with everyone joining.
